claim: The model is built on mesoscopic connectome data for interareal cortical connections.
source: The model is built on mesoscopic connectome data for interareal cortical connections and endowed with a macroscopic gradient of measured parvalbumin-expressing interneuron density.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the model uses mesoscopic connectome data.

claim: The model is endowed with a macroscopic gradient of measured parvalbumin-expressing interneuron density.
source: The model is built on mesoscopic connectome data for interareal cortical connections and endowed with a macroscopic gradient of measured parvalbumin-expressing interneuron density.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the model incorporates measured PV interneuron density gradients.

claim: Working memory coding is distributed yet exhibits modularity.
source: We found that working memory coding is distributed yet exhibits modularity; the spatial pattern of mnemonic representation is determined by long-range cell type-specific targeting and density of cell classes.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the model.

claim: The spatial pattern of mnemonic representation is determined by long-range cell type-specific targeting and density of cell classes.
source: We found that working memory coding is distributed yet exhibits modularity; the spatial pattern of mnemonic representation is determined by long-range cell type-specific targeting and density of cell classes.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the model.

claim: Cell type-specific graph measures predict the activity patterns and a core subnetwork for memory maintenance.
source: Cell type-specific graph measures predict the activity patterns and a core subnetwork for memory maintenance.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the model.

claim: The model shows numerous attractor states, which are self-sustained internal states (each engaging a distinct subset of areas).
source: The model shows numerous attractor states, which are self-sustained internal states (each engaging a distinct subset of areas).
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the model.

claim: Working memory is the brain's ability to internally hold and process information without sensory input.
source: We developed a large-scale model of the multiregional mouse brain for a cardinal cognitive function called working memory, the brain's ability to internally hold and process information without sensory input.
evidence: This is a standard definition of working memory provided in the abstract.

claim: Delay-period mnemonic persistent neural activity has been observed in multiple brain regions.
source: Delay-period mnemonic persistent neural activity has been observed in multiple brain regions, suggesting a distributed working memory representation (Suzuki and Gottlieb, 2013; Leavitt et al., 2017; Christophel et al., 2017; Xu, 2017; Dotson et al., 2018, also see Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Connectome-based computational models of the macaque cortex found that working memory activity depends on interareal connectivity.
source: Connectome-based computational models of the macaque cortex found that working memory activity depends on interareal connectivity (Murray et al., 2017; Jaramillo et al., 2019), macroscopic gradients of synaptic excitation (Wang, 2020; Mejías and Wang, 2022), and dopamine modulation (Froudist-Walsh et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Connectome-based computational models of the macaque cortex found that working memory activity depends on macroscopic gradients of synaptic excitation.
source: Connectome-based computational models of the macaque cortex found that working memory activity depends on interareal connectivity (Murray et al., 2017; Jaramillo et al., 2019), macroscopic gradients of synaptic excitation (Wang, 2020; Mejías and Wang, 2022), and dopamine modulation (Froudist-Walsh et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Connectome-based computational models of the macaque cortex found that working memory activity depends on dopamine modulation.
source: Connectome-based computational models of the macaque cortex found that working memory activity depends on interareal connectivity (Murray et al., 2017; Jaramillo et al., 2019), macroscopic gradients of synaptic excitation (Wang, 2020; Mejías and Wang, 2022), and dopamine modulation (Froudist-Walsh et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Mnemonic neural activity during a delay period is distributed in the mouse brain.
source: Mnemonic neural activity during a delay period is also distributed in the mouse brain (Liu et al., 2014; Schmitt et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017; Bolkan et al., 2017; Gilad et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claim: In the monkey cortex, the number of spines per pyramidal cell increases along the cortical hierarchy.
source: In the monkey cortex, the number of spines (sites of excitatory synapses) per pyramidal cell increases along the cortical hierarchy, consistent with the idea that mnemonic persistent activity in association cortical areas including the prefrontal cortex is sustained by recurrent excitation that is stronger than in early sensory areas.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about monkey cortex anatomy.

claim: Such a macroscopic gradient is lacking in the mouse cortex.
source: Such a macroscopic gradient is lacking in the mouse cortex (Gilman et al., 2017; Ballesteros-Yáñez et al., 2010), raising the possibility that the brain mechanism for distributed working memory representations may be fundamentally different between mice and monkeys.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: The model is built on the recently available mesoscopic connectivity data of the mouse thalamocortical system.
source: We developed an anatomically-based model of the mouse brain for working memory, built on the recently available mesoscopic connectivity data of the mouse thalamocortical system (Oh et al., 2014; Gămănut et al., 2018; Harris et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction states the model uses specific connectivity datasets.

claim: The model is validated by capturing large-scale neural activity observed in recent mouse experiments.
source: Our model is validated by capturing large-scale neural activity observed in recent mouse experiments (Guo et al., 2017; Gilad et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction states the model reproduces experimental observations.

claim: A decreasing gradient of synaptic inhibition mediated by parvalbumin (PV)-positive GABAergic cells and long-range excitatory connections shapes the distributed pattern of working memory representation.
source: Using this model, we found that a decreasing gradient of synaptic inhibition mediated by parvalbumin (PV)-positive GABAergic cells (Kim et al., 2017; Fulcher et al., 2019; Wang, 2020) and long-range excitatory connections shapes the distributed pattern of working memory representation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the model.

claim: Traditional graph-theory measures of interareal connections, which ignore cell types of projection targets, are uncorrelated with activity patterns.
source: Interestingly, traditional graph-theory measures of interareal connections, which ignore cell types of projection targets, are uncorrelated with activity patterns.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Cell type-specific graph theory measures can differentiate contributions of cortical areas in terms of their distinct roles in loading, maintaining, and reading out the content of working memory.
source: We propose new cell type-specific graph theory measures to overcome this problem and differentiate contributions of cortical areas in terms of their distinct roles in loading, maintaining, and reading out the content of working memory.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological contribution of the work.

claim: A core subnetwork was uncovered for the generation of persistent activity through computer-simulated perturbations akin to optogenetic inactivations.
source: Through computer-simulated perturbations akin to optogenetic inactivations, a core subnetwork was uncovered for the generation of persistent activity.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the model simulations.

claim: This core subnetwork can be predicted based on the cell type-specific interareal connectivity.
source: This core subnetwork can be predicted based on the cell type-specific interareal connectivity, highlighting the necessity of knowing the cell type targets of interareal connections in order to relate anatomy with physiology and behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the model analysis.

claim: The large-scale circuit model of the mouse cortex uses interareal connectivity provided by anatomical data within the 43-area parcellation in the common coordinate framework v3 atlas.
source: Our large-scale circuit model of the mouse cortex uses interareal connectivity provided by anatomical data within the 43-area parcellation in the common coordinate framework v3 atlas (Oh et al., 2014; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the anatomical basis of the model with reference to data and figures.

claim: The model is endowed with area-to-area variation of PV-expressing interneurons in the form of a gradient measured from the qBrain mapping platform.
source: The model is endowed with area-to-area variation of PV-expressing interneurons in the form of a gradient measured from the qBrain mapping platform (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model with reference to data source.

claim: Primary sensory areas have a higher density of PV interneurons than association areas.
source: Therefore, primary sensory areas have a higher density of PV interneurons than association areas, although the gradient of PV interneurons does not align perfectly with the cortical hierarchy.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The gradient of PV interneurons does not align perfectly with the cortical hierarchy.
source: Therefore, primary sensory areas have a higher density of PV interneurons than association areas, although the gradient of PV interneurons does not align perfectly with the cortical hierarchy.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There is a moderate negative correlation between PV cell fraction and cortical hierarchy (Pearson correlation coefficient r = –0.35, p<0.05).
source: In Figure 1F, the PV cell fraction is plotted as a function of the cortical hierarchy, which shows a moderate negative correlation between the two.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1F with statistical values.

claim: Each cortical area is described by a local circuit using a mean-field reduction of a spiking neural network.
source: In our model, each cortical area is described by a local circuit (Figure 2A) using a mean-field reduction (Wong and Wang, 2006) of a spiking neural network (Wang, 2002).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach with citations to prior methods.

claim: Each cortical area contains two excitatory neural pools selective for different stimuli and a shared inhibitory neural pool.
source: Specifically, each cortical area contains two excitatory neural pools selective for different stimuli and a shared inhibitory neural pool.
evidence: This describes the structure of the local circuit model.

claim: Local inhibitory strength is proportional to PV interneuron density across the cortex.
source: The model makes the following assumptions. First, local inhibitory strength is proportional to PV interneuron density across the cortex.
evidence: This is stated as an explicit assumption of the model.

claim: The interareal long-range connection matrix is given by the anterograde tracing data.
source: Second, the interareal long-range connection matrix is given by the anterograde tracing data (Oh et al., 2014; Knox et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an explicit assumption of the model with citations.

claim: Targeting is biased onto inhibitory cells for top-down compared with bottom-up projections.
source: Third, targeting is biased onto inhibitory cells for top-down compared with bottom-up projections.
evidence: This is stated as an explicit assumption of the model.

claim: Feedforward connections have a greater net excitatory effect than feedback connections, which is referred to as the counterstream inhibitory bias (CIB).
source: Therefore, feedforward connections have a greater net excitatory effect than feedback connections, which is referred to as the counterstream inhibitory bias (CIB) (Mejías and Wang, 2022; Javadzadeh and Hofer, 2022; Wang, 2022).
evidence: This defines a key concept in the model with citations.

claim: After removal of the external stimulus, the firing rate in area VISp decreases rapidly to baseline.
source: After removal of the external stimulus, the firing rate in area VISp decreases rapidly to baseline.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Many frontal and lateral areas (including prelimbic [PL], infralimbic [ILA], secondary motor [MOs], and ventral agranular insula [AIv] areas) sustained a high firing rate during the delay period.
source: In stark contrast, many frontal and lateral areas (including prelimbic [PL], infralimbic [ILA], secondary motor [MOs], and ventral agranular insula [AIv] areas) sustained a high firing rate during the delay period (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Areas that are higher in the cortical hierarchy show elevated activity during the delay period.
source: Areas that are higher in the cortical hierarchy show elevated activity during the delay period (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: This persistent firing rate could last for more than 10 s and is a stable attractor state of the network.
source: This persistent firing rate could last for more than 10 s and is a stable attractor state of the network (Inagaki et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the model with a citation to experimental work.

claim: The cortical hierarchy and PV fraction predict the delay-period firing rate of each cortical area.
source: The cortical hierarchy and PV fraction predict the delay-period firing rate of each cortical area (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the model analysis shown in Figures 2C-E.

claim: The delay activity pattern has a stronger correlation with hierarchy (r = 0.91) than with the PV fraction (r = –0.43).
source: The delay activity pattern has a stronger correlation with hierarchy (r = 0.91) than with the PV fraction (r = –0.43).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from the model analysis.

claim: The long-range connections play a predominant important role in defining the persistent activity pattern.
source: Thus the activity pattern of distributed working memory depends on both local and large-scale anatomy. The delay activity pattern has a stronger correlation with hierarchy (r = 0.91) than with the PV fraction (r = –0.43). The long-range connections thus play a predominant important role in defining the persistent activity pattern.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the correlation analysis.

claim: When the delay-period firing rates are plotted versus hierarchy, there is a gap in the distribution of persistent activity that marks an abrupt transition in the cortical space.
source: When the delay-period firing rates are plotted versus hierarchy, we observe a gap in the distribution of persistent activity (Figure 2D) that marks an abrupt transition in the cortical space.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the model analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: This leads to the emergence of a subnetwork of areas capable of working memory representations.
source: This leads to the emergence of a subnetwork of areas capable of working memory representations.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observed gap in firing rates.

claim: The pattern of delay-period firing rates for somatosensory and auditory sensory modalities is similar to the results obtained for the visual task.
source: The pattern of delay-period firing rates for these sensory modalities is similar to the results obtained for the visual task: sensory areas show transient activity, while frontal and lateral areas show persistent activity after stimulus withdrawal.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from additional model simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cortical hierarchy could predict the delay-period firing rate of each cortical area well (r = 0.89, p<0.05) for somatosensory and auditory tasks.
source: Moreover, the cortical hierarchy could predict the delay-period firing rate of each cortical area well (r = 0.89, p<0.05), while the PV cell fraction could also predict the delay-period firing rate of each cortical area with a smaller correlation coefficient (r = –0.4, p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from additional model simulations.

claim: Working memory may share common activation patterns across sensory modalities.
source: Our model thus predicts that working memory may share common activation patterns across sensory modalities, which is partially supported by cortical recordings during a memory-guided response task (Inagaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model with a citation to supporting experimental work.

claim: When the PV gradient is replaced with a constant value, the number of cortical areas displaying persistent activity is diminished, but the abrupt transition in delay-period firing rates remains.
source: As compared to the model with a PV gradient (Figure 3A(i)), we found that, during the delay period, the number of cortical areas displaying persistent activity is diminished, but the abrupt transition in delay-period firing rates remains.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from model manipulations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When CIB is removed by scaling feedforward and feedback projections with a constant value across areas, the firing rate of both sensory and association areas exhibit high firing rates during the delay period.
source: Next, we performed the analogous manipulation on the CIB by scaling feedforward and feedback projections with a constant value across areas, thus effectively removing the CIB. In this case, the firing rate of both sensory and association areas exhibit high firing rates during the delay period (Figure 3A(iii)).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from model manipulations shown in Figure 3A(iii).

claim: CIB may be particularly important in determining which areas exhibit persistent activity.
source: Thus, CIB may be particularly important in determining which areas exhibit persistent activity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the model manipulations.

claim: If PV cell fraction is not strongly correlated with delay firing rate across cortical areas, this suggests the existence of a CIB mechanism at play.
source: This observation led to a model prediction: if PV cell fraction is not strongly correlated with delay firing rate across cortical areas (e.g., Figure 3A(i) or Figure 3B(i)), this suggests the existence of a CIB mechanism at play.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model analysis.

claim: The model without CIB exhibits the abrupt transition in delay-period firing rates provided it is in a regime where some areas exhibit 'independent' persistent activity.
source: Importantly, the model without CIB exhibits the abrupt transition in delay-period firing rates provided it is in a regime where some areas exhibit 'independent' persistent activity: persistent activity that is generated due to local recurrence and thus independent of long-range recurrent loops.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from model analysis across parameter regimes.

claim: CIB may be particularly important in the regime where local connections are not sufficient to sustain independent persistent activity.
source: To conclude, the model results suggest that CIB may be present in a large-scale brain network if the PV cell fraction is not strongly correlated with the delay firing rate. Furthermore, CIB may be particularly important in the regime where local connections are not sufficient to sustain independent persistent activity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: While PV and CIB shape the distribution of delay firing rates across cortical areas, they do not qualitatively influence the system's baseline stability.
source: Thus, while PV and CIB shape the distribution of delay firing rates across cortical areas, they do not qualitatively influence the system's baseline stability.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the stability analysis shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The inclusion of both PV gradient and CIB in the model results in a more robust system, that is, a far wider set of parameters can produce realistic persistent activity.
source: However, the inclusion of both PV gradient and CIB in the model (Figure 3C) results in a more robust system, that is, a far wider set of parameters can produce realistic persistent activity (Figure 3C, D and E).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the parameter exploration shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Individual local networks without long-range connections are stable without local inhibition.
source: We found that individual local networks without long-range connections are stable without local inhibition (Figure 4A, see 'Methods' for theoretical calculation of stability in a local circuit).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from stability analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the full network with long-range connections, setting either the long-range connections to inhibitory neurons or local inhibition to zero made the network's baseline state unstable.
source: However, in the full network with long-range connections, setting either the long-range connections to inhibitory neurons or local inhibition to zero made the network's baseline state unstable, and individual areas rose to a high firing rate (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from stability analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Inhibition from local and long-range circuits contributes to the baseline stability of cortical areas.
source: Thus, inhibition from local and long-range circuits contributes to the baseline stability of cortical areas.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the stability analysis.

claim: The network is in a 'global' ISN regime, whereby long-range connections to inhibitory neurons are necessary to maintain a stable baseline state.
source: Thus we propose that the network is also in a 'global' ISN regime, whereby long-range connections to inhibitory neurons are necessary to maintain a stable baseline state.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the stability analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The interconnected ISN networks are compatible with bistability of a subset of cortical areas.
source: When we considered the full network with long-range projections, the network exhibits a graded firing rate pattern after transient stimulation of VISp, showing that the interconnected ISN networks are compatible with bistability of a subset of cortical areas (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the model analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Distinct local and long-range inhibitory mechanisms shape the pattern of working memory activity and stability of the baseline state.
source: In summary, we have shown that distinct local and long-range inhibitory mechanisms shape the pattern of working memory activity and stability of the baseline state.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Several studies have shown that thalamic areas are also involved in the maintenance of working memory.
source: Several studies have shown that thalamic areas are also involved in the maintenance of working memory (Bolkan et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017; Schmitt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The large-scale thalamocortical mechanisms underlying memory maintenance are unknown.
source: However, the large-scale thalamocortical mechanisms underlying memory maintenance are unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the thalamocortical model.

claim: There are no recurrent connections in the thalamus within or across thalamic nuclei.
source: There are no recurrent connections in the thalamus within or across thalamic nuclei (Jones, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as an anatomical fact with a citation.

claim: Persistent activity can still be generated but is maintained with the help of the thalamocortical loop.
source: Here, we weakened the strength of cortical interareal connections as compared to the cortex model of Figure 2. Now, persistent activity can still be generated (Figure 5B, blue) but is maintained with the help of the thalamocortical loop, as observed experimentally (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the thalamocortical model with a citation to experimental work.

claim: In simulations where the thalamus was inactivated, the cortical network no longer showed sustained activity.
source: Indeed, in simulations where the thalamus was inactivated, the cortical network no longer showed sustained activity (Figure 5B, red).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the thalamocortical model simulation shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the thalamocortical model, the delay activity pattern of the cortical areas correlates with the hierarchy, again with a gap in the firing rate separating the areas engaged in persistent activity from those that do not.
source: In the thalamocortical model, the delay activity pattern of the cortical areas correlates with the hierarchy, again with a gap in the firing rate separating the areas engaged in persistent activity from those that do not (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the thalamocortical model shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The firing rate of thalamic areas continuously increases along the hierarchy.
source: Unlike the cortex, the firing rate of thalamic areas continuously increases along the hierarchy (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the thalamocortical model shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The delay-period firing rate of cortical areas in the thalamocortical model correlates well with the firing rate of the same areas in the cortical model.
source: Furthermore, the delay-period firing rate of cortical areas in the thalamocortical model correlates well with the firing rate of the same areas in the cortical model (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from comparing the two models shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The cortical model captures most of the dynamical properties in the thalamocortical model.
source: This comparison suggests that the cortical model captures most of the dynamical properties in the thalamocortical model; therefore in the following analyses, we will mainly focus on the cortex-only model for simplicity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparison between models.

claim: Standard graph theory measures could not predict the pattern of delay-period firing across areas.
source: Structural connectivity constrains large-scale dynamics (Mejías and Wang, 2022; Froudist-Walsh et al., 2021; Cabral et al., 2011). However, we found that standard graph theory measures could not predict the pattern of delay-period firing across areas.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the graph theory analysis.

claim: There is no significant correlation between input strength and delay-period firing rate (r = 0.25, p=0.25).
source: There is no significant correlation between input strength (the total weight of all interareal input connections to an area) and delay-period firing rate (r = 0.25, p=0.25, Figure 6A(i) and (ii)) and input strength cannot predict which areas show persistent activity (prediction accuracy = 0.51, Figure 6A(iii)).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from the graph theory analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Input strength cannot predict which areas show persistent activity (prediction accuracy = 0.51).
source: There is no significant correlation between input strength (the total weight of all interareal input connections to an area) and delay-period firing rate (r = 0.25, p=0.25, Figure 6A(i) and (ii)) and input strength cannot predict which areas show persistent activity (prediction accuracy = 0.51, Figure 6A(iii)).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from the graph theory analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cell type specificity of interareal connections must be taken into account in order to relate the connectome with the whole-brain dynamics and function.
source: Therefore, cell type specificity of interareal connections must be taken into account in order to relate the connectome with the whole-brain dynamics and function.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the graph theory analysis.

claim: The cell type-specific input strength has a strong correlation with delay-period firing rate of cortical areas showing persistent activity (r = 0.89, p<0.05).
source: Cell type-specific input strength has a strong correlation with delay-period firing rate of cortical areas showing persistent activity (r = 0.89, p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from the cell type-specific graph theory analysis shown in Figure 6B(ii).

claim: Cell type-specific input strength accurately predicts which areas show persistent activity (prediction accuracy = 0.95).
source: Cell type-specific input strength also accurately predicts which areas show persistent activity (Figure 6B(iii)).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from the cell type-specific graph theory analysis shown in Figure 6B(iii).

claim: The cell type-specific eigenvector centrality, but not standard eigenvector centrality, was a good predictor of delay-period firing rates.
source: Similarly, we found that the cell type-specific eigenvector centrality, but not standard eigenvector centrality (Newman, 2018), was a good predictor of delay-period firing rates (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the graph theory analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inactivation of an area like VISp impairs performance of a delay-dependent task because it is essential for a (visual) 'input' to access working memory.
source: For instance, inactivation of an area like VISp impairs performance of a delay-dependent task because it is essential for a (visual) 'input' to access working memory; on the other hand, a 'readout' area may display persistent activity only as a result of sustained inputs from other areas that form a 'core,' which are causally important for maintaining a memory representation.
evidence: This is stated as a conceptual distinction between area types.

claim: Core areas form recurrent loops and support distributed persistent activity across the network.
source: Core areas form recurrent loops and support distributed persistent activity across the network. By definition, disrupting any of the core areas would affect persistent activity globally.
evidence: This is stated as a definition of core areas.

claim: Disrupting any of the core areas would affect persistent activity globally.
source: Core areas form recurrent loops and support distributed persistent activity across the network. By definition, disrupting any of the core areas would affect persistent activity globally.
evidence: This is stated as a defining property of core areas.

claim: Inhibiting readout areas has little effect on persistent activity elsewhere in the network.
source: The readout areas also show persistent activity. Yet, inhibiting readout areas has little effect on persistent activity elsewhere in the network.
evidence: This is stated as a defining property of readout areas.

claim: Seven areas were identified with a substantial inhibition effect during the delay period, which are identified as a core for working memory.
source: We identified seven areas with a substantial inhibition effect during the delay period (Figure 7C), which we identify as a core for working memory.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the inhibition analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Core areas are distributed across the cortex and include frontal areas PL, ILA, medial part of the orbital area (ORBm), which are known to contribute to working memory.
source: Core areas are distributed across the cortex. They include frontal areas PL, ILA, medial part of the orbital area (ORBm), which are known to contribute to working memory (Liu et al., 2014; Bolkan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the inhibition analysis with citations to prior work.

claim: Other associative and sensory areas (AId, VISpm, ectorhinal area [ECT], gustatory area [GU]) are also in the core.
source: Other associative and sensory areas (AId, VISpm, ectorhinal area [ECT], gustatory area [GU]) are also in the core.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the inhibition analysis.

claim: After inhibiting a pair of readout areas, there was a decrement in the average firing rate of the network.
source: We first inhibited pairs of readout areas and evaluated the effect of this manipulation at a network level. Specifically, for any given readout area A, we plotted the average firing rate of the network when A was inhibited as part of an inhibited pair (see description in 'Methods'). After inhibiting a pair of readout areas, there was a decrement in the average firing rate of the network (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the multiple area inhibition analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The decrement became more pronounced as more readout areas were inhibited, for example, triplets and quadruplets.
source: The decrement became more pronounced as more readout areas were inhibited, for example, triplets and quadruplets, and when a combination of readout and core areas was inhibited pairwise (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the multiple area inhibition analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Readout areas also play a role in maintaining distributed persistent activity.
source: This analysis demonstrates that readout areas also play a role in maintaining distributed persistent activity: we may define 'second-order core areas' as those readout areas that have a strong inhibition effect only when inhibited concurrently with another area, while third-order and fourth-order core areas are analogously defined via triplet and quadruplet inhibition, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the multiple area inhibition analysis.

claim: After inhibiting all core areas, there was a 48% decrement in the average firing rate compared with a 15% decrement for a single core area and a 3% decrement for a single readout area.
source: We also tested the effect of inhibiting all core areas during the delay period (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C). After inhibiting all core areas, some readout areas lost persistent firing. Moreover, there was a 48% decrement in the average firing rate compared with a 15% decrement for a single core area and a 3% decrement for a single readout area.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from the inhibition analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The pattern of persistent activity is more sensitive to perturbations of core areas, which underscores the classification of some cortical areas into core vs readout.
source: Thus, the pattern of persistent activity is more sensitive to perturbations of core areas, which underscores the classification of some cortical areas into core vs readout.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the inhibition analysis.

claim: In the dynamical regime where individual cortical areas do not show persistent activity independently, distributed working memory patterns must be a result of long-range recurrent loops across areas.
source: In the dynamical regime where individual cortical areas do not show persistent activity independently, distributed working memory patterns must be a result of long-range recurrent loops across areas.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference about the mechanism.

claim: The cell type-specific loop strength, but not the raw loop strength, predicts which area is a core area with high accuracy (prediction accuracy = 0.93).
source: The cell type-specific loop strength, but not the raw loop strength, predicts which area is a core area with high accuracy (Figure 8D(i) and (ii), prediction accuracy = 0.93).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from the loop strength analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Traditional connectivity measures are informative but not sufficient to explain dynamics during cognition in the mouse brain.
source: This demonstrates that traditional connectivity measures are informative but not sufficient to explain dynamics during cognition in the mouse brain.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the loop strength analysis.

claim: Cell type-specific connectivity, and new metrics that account for such connectivity, are necessary to infer the role of brain areas in supporting large-scale brain dynamics during cognition.
source: Cell type-specific connectivity, and new metrics that account for such connectivity, are necessary to infer the role of brain areas in supporting large-scale brain dynamics during cognition.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Different tasks lead to dissociable patterns of internally sustained activity across the brain, described dynamically as distinct attractor states.
source: Different tasks lead to dissociable patterns of internally sustained activity across the brain, described dynamically as distinct attractor states.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle about attractor states.

claim: Attractor states may enable computations such as decision making and working memory.
source: Generally, attractor states may enable computations such as decision making and working memory (Wang, 1999; Wang, 2002; Mejias et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a general principle with citations.

claim: Increasing the long-range connection strength decreases the number of attractors.
source: Increasing the long-range connection strength decreases the number of attractors (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the attractor analysis shown in Figure 9D.

claim: When the local excitatory strength is increased, the number of attractors increased as well.
source: When the local excitatory strength is increased, the number of attractors increased as well (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the attractor analysis shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Local and long-range connection strength have opposite effects on the number of attractors.
source: Thus, local and long-range connection strength have opposite effects on the number of attractors.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the attractor analysis.

claim: The cell type-specific input strength predicted firing rates across many attractors.
source: The cell type-specific input strength predicted firing rates across many attractors.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the attractor analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: The raw input strength is weakly correlated with activity patterns across attractors.
source: The raw input strength is weakly correlated with activity patterns.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the attractor analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: The cell type-specific input strength is strongly correlated with activity across attractors.
source: The cell type-specific input strength is strongly correlated with activity across attractors.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the attractor analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Different attractor states rely on distinct subsets of core areas.
source: Different attractor states rely on distinct subsets of core areas.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the attractor analysis.

claim: MOs shows strong persistent activity during delay period and is consistent with its role in short-term memory and planning.
source: MOs also showed strong persistent activity during delay period. This is consistent with its role in short-term memory and planning (Li et al., 2015; Inagaki et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with citations to prior work.

claim: The cell type-specific loop strength was the strongest in area MOs for the example attractor.
source: To calculate a loop strength that was specific to this attractor, we only examined connections between these five areas. The cell type-specific loop strength was the strongest in area MOs (Figure 9I).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the attractor-specific loop strength analysis shown in Figure 9I.

claim: We can identify likely core areas for individual attractor states from cell type-specific structural measures.
source: Thus, we can identify likely core areas for individual attractor states from cell type-specific structural measures.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the attractor-specific analysis.

claim: Different attractor states can be supported by distinct core areas.
source: This also demonstrates that different attractor states can be supported by distinct core areas.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the attractor analysis.

claim: This is the first biologically based model of the entire mouse cortex and the thalamocortical system that supports a cognitive function, in this case working memory.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first biologically based model of the entire mouse cortex and the thalamocortical system that supports a cognitive function, in this case working memory.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: The mnemonic activity pattern is shaped by the differing densities of PV interneurons across cortical areas.
source: First, the mnemonic activity pattern is shaped by the differing densities of PV interneurons across cortical areas.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the Discussion.

claim: Areas with a high PV cell fraction encoded information only transiently, while those with low PV cell fraction sustained activity for longer periods.
source: Areas with a high PV cell fraction encoded information only transiently, while those with low PV cell fraction sustained activity for longer periods.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the Discussion.

claim: The gradient of PV cells has a definitive role in separating rapid information processing in sensory areas from sustained mnemonic information representation in associative areas of the mouse cortex.
source: Thus, the gradient of PV cells (Kim et al., 2017) has a definitive role in separating rapid information processing in sensory areas from sustained mnemonic information representation in associative areas of the mouse cortex.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion with a citation.

claim: Each local area operates in the 'inhibition-stabilizing regime' where recurrent excitation alone would lead to instability but the local network is stabilized by feedback inhibition.
source: This is consistent with the view that each local area operates in the 'inhibition-stabilizing regime' where recurrent excitation alone would lead to instability but the local network is stabilized by feedback inhibition, which may arise from long-range excitatory inputs to inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The concept of synaptic reverberation is extended to the large-scale global brain.
source: Thereby the concept of synaptic reverberation (de NÓ, 1933; Wang, 2001; Wang, 2021) is extended to the large-scale global brain.
evidence: This is stated as a conceptual contribution with citations.

claim: Currently it is unclear whether persistent neural firing observed in a delay dependent task is generated locally or depends on long-distance reverberation among multiple brain regions.
source: Note that currently it is unclear whether persistent neural firing observed in a delay dependent task is generated locally or depends on long-distance reverberation among multiple brain regions.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: Presently available connectomic data are not sufficient to account for neural dynamics and distributed cognition.
source: Third, presently available connectomic data are not sufficient to account for neural dynamics and distributed cognition, and we propose cell type-specific connectomic measures that are shown to predict the observed distributed working memory representations.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the Discussion.

claim: Although connectome databases are an invaluable resource for basic neuroscience, they should be supplemented with cell type-specific information.
source: Our model underscores that, although connectome databases are an invaluable resource for basic neuroscience, they should be supplemented with cell type-specific information.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the work.

claim: Recurrent loops within the cortex and the thalamocortical network aided in sustaining activity throughout the delay period.
source: We found that recurrent loops within the cortex and the thalamocortical network aided in sustaining activity throughout the delay period (Guo et al., 2017; Schmitt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with citations to prior work.

claim: The specific pattern of cortico-cortical connections was critical to working memory.
source: The specific pattern of cortico-cortical connections was also critical to working memory.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: By focusing on cell type-specific interactions between areas, we were able to reveal a core of cortical areas connected by excitatory loops and responsible for generating a widely distributed pattern of sustained activity.
source: By focusing on cell type-specific interactions between areas, we were able to reveal a core of cortical areas. The core is connected by excitatory loops and is responsible for generating a widely distributed pattern of sustained activity.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: This clarifies the synergistic roles of the connectome and gradients of local circuit properties in producing a distributed cognitive function.
source: This clarifies the synergistic roles of the connectome and gradients of local circuit properties in producing a distributed cognitive function.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion.

claim: In the macaque cortex the density of spines on pyramidal cells increases along the cortical hierarchy.
source: These models consider the fact that in the macaque cortex the density of spines on pyramidal cells increases along the cortical hierarchy (Elston and Rosa, 1998; Elston, 2007; Chaudhuri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with citations.

claim: Such excitatory gradients based on spine count are less pronounced and may be entirely absent in the rodent cortex.
source: Such excitatory gradients based on spine count are less pronounced and may be entirely absent in the rodent cortex (Ballesteros-Yáñez et al., 2010; Gilman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with citations.

claim: There are gradients of synaptic inhibition in the mouse cortex.
source: However, there are gradients of synaptic inhibition in the mouse cortex (Kim et al., 2017; Wang, 2021).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with citations.

claim: Spatially distributed persistent-activity patterns in the mouse cortex do not require gradients of recurrent excitation.
source: We have used this gradient of inhibition in our model to show that spatially distributed persistent-activity patterns in the mouse cortex do not require gradients of recurrent excitation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the model.

claim: Local recurrency in the mouse early sensory areas is higher than in the primate.
source: Along these lines, we predict that local recurrency in the mouse early sensory areas is higher than in the primate.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model.

claim: Both the spine density and the number of excitatory and inhibitory synapses in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in area V1 are higher in mouse compared to macaque.
source: Consistent with this claim, both the spine density and the number of excitatory and inhibitory synapses in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in area V1 are higher in mouse compared to macaque (Figure 5A in Gilman et al., 2017 and Figure 1A in Wildenberg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as supporting evidence for the prediction with citations.

claim: The macaque cortex is a densely connected graph at an inter-area level, with the connectivity spanning five orders of magnitude.
source: In the language of network theory, the macaque cortex is a densely connected graph at an inter-area level, with the connectivity spanning five orders of magnitude (Markov et al., 2014b), which is more than what is expected for small-world networks (Bassett and Bullmore, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with citations.

claim: The mouse 'connectome' has even denser area-to-area connections than the macaque.
source: Critically, the mouse 'connectome' (e.g., Oh et al., 2014; Harris et al., 2019; Knox et al., 2019) has even denser area-to-area connections.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with citations.

claim: In the visual cortex, individual neurons target more cortical areas in the mouse and they have more inhibitory and excitatory synapses.
source: In the visual cortex, individual neurons target more cortical areas in the mouse (Siu et al., 2021) and they have more inhibitory and excitatory synapses (Wildenberg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with citations.

claim: Connectivity in the mouse is denser at both the area and single-cell levels (at least for primary visual cortex).
source: Thus, connectivity in the mouse is denser at both the area and single-cell levels (at least for primary visual cortex).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the cited evidence.

claim: There is a greater functional specialization in the primate cortex which is afforded by the sparser and more targeted patterns of connectivity at the single-cell and area levels.
source: We propose that there is a greater functional specialization in the primate cortex which is afforded by the sparser and more targeted patterns of connectivity at the single-cell and area levels.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the connectivity differences.

claim: The ratio of NMDA to AMPA-mediated synaptic currents is approximately constant in the mouse cortex.
source: Other differences to explore in future computational models include the ratio of NMDA to AMPA-mediated synaptic currents, which is approximately constant in the mouse cortex (Myme et al., 2003) but varies along the cortical hierarchy in primates (Yang et al., 2018; Klatzmann et al., 2022), as well as hierarchy, which is defined based on feedforward and feedback projections in the mouse (Harris et al., 2019) and primate (Markov et al., 2014a; Markov et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with citations.

claim: The ratio of NMDA to AMPA-mediated synaptic currents varies along the cortical hierarchy in primates.
source: Other differences to explore in future computational models include the ratio of NMDA to AMPA-mediated synaptic currents, which is approximately constant in the mouse cortex (Myme et al., 2003) but varies along the cortical hierarchy in primates (Yang et al., 2018; Klatzmann et al., 2022), as well as hierarchy, which is defined based on feedforward and feedback projections in the mouse (Harris et al., 2019) and primate (Markov et al., 2014a; Markov et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with citations.

claim: Traditional graph theory metrics of connectivity were unable to predict the working memory activity in the mouse brain.
source: We found that traditional graph theory metrics of connectivity were unable to predict the working memory activity in the mouse brain.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: This may be due to the almost fully connected pattern of interareal connectivity in the mouse cortex.
source: This may be due to the almost fully connected pattern of interareal connectivity in the mouse cortex (Gămănut et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation with a citation.

claim: Feedforward connections had a greater net excitatory effect than feedback connections, a hypothesis which is referred to as CIB.
source: Specifically, feedforward connections had a greater net excitatory effect than feedback connections, a hypothesis which we refer to as CIB.
evidence: This is stated as a model assumption.

claim: This preferential targeting of feedback projections serves to stabilize the otherwise excitable activity of sensory areas and is consistent with recent experiments that report long-range recruitment of GABAergic neurons in early sensory areas.
source: This preferential targeting of feedback projections serves to stabilize the otherwise excitable activity of sensory areas (Mejías and Wang, 2022) and is consistent with recent experiments that report long-range recruitment of GABAergic neurons in early sensory areas (Campagnola et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022; Naskar et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citations to supporting experimental work.

claim: If there is a weak correlation between PV cell density and delay firing rate across cortical areas, then the CIB mechanism is at play.
source: Our model predicts that if there is a weak correlation between PV cell density and delay firing rate across cortical areas, then the CIB mechanism is at play.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model.

claim: CIB is particularly important in the regime where local connections are not sufficient to sustain spatially patterned persistent activity.
source: Moreover, the model results suggest that CIB is particularly important in the regime where local connections are not sufficient to sustain spatially patterned persistent activity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: There are parameter regimes where CIB becomes less important, provided there is a gradient of synaptic inhibition as in the mouse cortex.
source: We also showed that there are parameter regimes where CIB becomes less important, provided there is a gradient of synaptic inhibition as in the mouse cortex (Kim et al., 2017, but see Nigro et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with citations.

claim: The model's resilience to parameter variations in inhibitory connection strengths is significantly enhanced when both the PV gradient and CIB are present.
source: Notably, the model's resilience to parameter variations in inhibitory connection strengths is significantly enhanced when both the PV gradient and CIB are present.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the parameter exploration.

claim: The inclusion of multiple inhibitory mechanisms that allow for connectivity variations might confer evolutionary advantages.
source: Given that working memory is a fundamental cognitive function observed across many individual brains with anatomical differences, the inclusion of multiple inhibitory mechanisms that allow for connectivity variations might confer evolutionary advantages.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about evolutionary implications.

claim: The manner in which long-range recurrent interactions affect neural dynamics depends not only on the existence of excitatory projections per se, but also on the target neurons' cell type.
source: To conclude, the manner in which long-range recurrent interactions affect neural dynamics depends not only on the existence of excitatory projections per se, but also on the target neurons' cell type.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion.

claim: For some cortical areas afferent long-range excitatory connections promote working memory-related activity while for some others, for example, early sensory areas, it does not.
source: Thus, for some cortical areas afferent long-range excitatory connections promote working memory-related activity while for some others, for example, early sensory areas, it does not.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion.

claim: The existence of long-range interactions is consistent with potentially distinct dynamical regimes.
source: Moreover, the existence of long-range interactions is consistent with potentially distinct dynamical regimes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion.

claim: By introducing cell type-specific graph theory metrics, we were able to predict the pattern and strength of delay period activity with high accuracy.
source: By introducing cell type-specific graph theory metrics, we were able to predict the pattern and strength of delay period activity with high accuracy.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: Cell type-specific graph-theory measures can accurately identify the core subnetwork, which can also be identified independently using a simulated large-scale optogenetic experiment.
source: Moreover, we demonstrated how cell type-specific graph-theory measures can accurately identify the core subnetwork, which can also be identified independently using a simulated large-scale optogenetic experiment.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: The core working memory subnetwork included frontal cortical areas with well-documented patterns of sustained activity during working memory tasks, such as prelimbic (PL), infralimbic (ILA), and medial orbitofrontal cortex (ORBm).
source: We found a core subnetwork of areas that, when inhibited, caused a substantial drop in activity in the remaining cortical areas. This core working memory subnetwork included frontal cortical areas with well-documented patterns of sustained activity during working memory tasks, such as prelimbic (PL), infralimbic (ILA), and medial orbitofrontal cortex (ORBm) (Schmitt et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with citations to prior work.

claim: The core subnetwork for the visual working memory task was distributed across the cortex and also included temporal and higher visual areas.
source: However, the core subnetwork for the visual working memory task we assessed was distributed across the cortex. It also included temporal and higher visual areas, suggesting that long-range recurrent connections between the frontal cortex and temporal and visual areas are responsible for generating persistent activity and maintaining visual information in working memory in the mouse.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: The gustatory area exhibits delay-period preparatory activity in a taste-guided decision-making task and inhibition of this area during the delay period impairs behavior.
source: For example, the gustatory area exhibits delay-period preparatory activity in a taste-guided decision-making task and inhibition of this area during the delay period impairs behavior (Vincis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as supporting evidence with a citation.

claim: MOs is a readout area and not a core area for visual working memory.
source: We also concluded that MOs is a readout area and not a core area.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the model.

claim: MOs is crucial for short-term memory maintenance, planning, and movement execution during a memory-guided response task.
source: This finding may be surprising considering previous studies that have shown this area to be crucial for short-term memory maintenance, planning, and movement execution during a memory-guided response task (Guo et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2014; Inagaki et al., 2019; Li et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2020; Voitov and Mrsic-Flogel, 2022).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: In the version of the memory-guided response task studied by Svoboda and others, short-term memory is conflated with movement preparation.
source: We note that in the version of the memory-guided response task studied by Svoboda and others, short-term memory is conflated with movement preparation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about prior work.

claim: Readout areas are not less important than core areas as readout areas can use the stored information for further computations and thus some readout areas are expected to be strongly coupled to behavior.
source: We emphasize that readout areas are not less important than core areas as readout areas can use the stored information for further computations and thus some readout areas are expected to be strongly coupled to behavior.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation.

claim: There is evidence for a differential engagement of cortical networks depending on the task design and on effectors.
source: Indeed, there is evidence for a differential engagement of cortical networks depending on the task design (Jonikaitis et al., 2023) and on effectors (Kubanek and Snyder, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: If ALM is indeed a readout area for sensory working memory tasks, then inhibiting ALM should have a relatively small effect on sustained activity in core areas (such as PL) during the delay period.
source: If ALM is indeed a readout area for sensory working memory tasks (e.g., Schmitt et al., 2017), then the following prediction arises. Inhibiting ALM should have a relatively small effect on sustained activity in core areas (such as PL) during the delay period.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction with a citation.

claim: Inhibiting PL and other core areas may disrupt sustained activity in ALM.
source: In contrast, inhibiting PL and other core areas may disrupt sustained activity in ALM.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction.

claim: ALM has a high cell type-specific loop strength, like that in core areas, which supports the possibility that it could form part of the core for motor preparation tasks.
source: Even if ALM is not part of the core for sensory working memory, it could form part of the core for motor preparation tasks (Figure 9G). We found a high cell type-specific loop strength for area ALM, like that in core areas, which supports this possibility (Figure 9I).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to figures.

claim: There are some attractor states for which the MOs was classified as a core area that do not contain area PL.
source: Furthermore, we found some attractor states for which the MOs was classified as a core area that do not contain area PL.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: There was no behavioral effect after PL inhibition in a motor planning task.
source: This result is supported by a recent study that found no behavioral effect after PL inhibition in a motor planning task (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as supporting evidence with a citation.

claim: The core subnetwork required for generating persistent activity is likely task-dependent.
source: Therefore, the core subnetwork required for generating persistent activity is likely task-dependent.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion.

claim: A large-scale inhibition protocol can identify the core subnetwork for a particular task.
source: We show that a large-scale inhibition protocol can identify the core subnetwork for a particular task.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: The core can be predicted based on the interareal loops that target excitatory neurons.
source: We further show how this core can be predicted based on the interareal loops that target excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: Were such a cell type-specific interareal connectivity dataset available, it may help interpretation of large-scale recording experiments.
source: Were such a cell type-specific interareal connectivity dataset available, it may help interpretation of large-scale recording experiments.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future applications.

claim: This could also focus circuit manipulation on regions most likely to cause an effect on the larger network activity and behavior.
source: This could also focus circuit manipulation on regions most likely to cause an effect on the larger network activity and behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future applications.

claim: The approach identifies the brain areas that work together to support working memory and those that benefit from such activity to serve other purposes.
source: Our approach identifies the brain areas that work together to support working memory. It also identifies those that benefit from such activity to serve other purposes.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the approach.

claim: The simulation and theoretical approach is ideally suited to understand the large-scale anatomy, recording, and manipulation experiments which are at the forefront of modern systems neuroscience.
source: Our simulation and theoretical approach is therefore ideally suited to understand the large-scale anatomy, recording, and manipulation experiments which are at the forefront of modern systems neuroscience.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the utility of the approach.
